paras: The threats against Henry Johnson in St. Louis took place on March 29, 1919, when a group of Marines confronted Sergeant Henry Johnson, a decorated Black soldier from Albany, New York, at his hotel and demanded that he retract remarks made in a speech the night before. After further threats by telephone, Johnson left the city that night in disguise, while returned white soldiers obtained a federal warrant against him.

Johnson made his first public appearance in St. Louis at the Coliseum on Friday, March 28, before a crowd that included white people in the box seats. Mayor Henry W. Kiel, Senator Selden P. Spencer, Congressman L. C. Dyer and other officials welcomed him.

In his speech Johnson described the prejudice Black soldiers suffered from white American soldiers and said he had to threaten to kill a white lieutenant who ran under fire. According to the St. Louis Argus, Black officers on the platform, among them Lieut. Geo. L. Vaughn, walked out, and Vaughn called him "undoubtedly crazy." The Cleveland Advocate described the speech as a "fiery account" in which he "denounced the white soldiers in France."

On Saturday afternoon, the Argus reported, about a dozen Marines came to the New Grand Hotel and threatened Johnson unless he took back what he had said about the cowardice of the Marines in France. Johnson refused, saying he had not charged the Marines with cowardice but had told the truth about the white lieutenant. Telephone calls and threats followed, and he left St. Louis that night in disguise.

A St. Louis dispatch dated March 29 gave a different account, stating that more than 100 marines, after a conference with Col. George K. Hunter at Jefferson Barracks, sent a committee of seven to demand that Johnson withdraw his charges. The same dispatch said a federal warrant was issued that day on the complaint of returned white soldiers, on the technical charge of wearing the uniform after a prescribed time.

Deputy marshals visited Johnson but deferred his arrest when, according to the dispatch, he promised to retract his charges in a formal statement. No report of an arrest, a retraction or Johnson's later movements appears in the coverage. Mrs. Victoria Clay-Haley, who had contracted to bring him to St. Louis, said he "did us more harm than good."

The St. Louis Argus gave the episode its fullest treatment, with a front-page headline deck reporting that the Marines threatened him at his hotel and that he “Is Compelled to Leave City in Disguise.” The same deck called Johnson "Unmanageable in Harangue," and the story stressed the embarrassment of the organizers and Black officers rather than the threats. An Argus editorial, "The Two Henry Johnsons," said it was a pity he lacked the sense to appreciate the honor offered him and urged readers to forget the matter.

Elsewhere in the Black press the story ran as a warrant item with no mention of the hotel threats. The Chicago Defender headlined it "White Soldiers Accuse Sergt. Johnson of Slander" on April 5, the Colorado Statesman carried one sentence the same day, and the Topeka Plaindealer printed the March 29 dispatch under "Called White Yanks Cowards" on April 11.

The Argus said Johnson refused to retract and denied accusing the Marines, while the dispatch said he promised a formal retraction and attributed to him the claim that the marines refused to fight in the same trenches as Black soldiers. The size of the Marine delegation also differs, from about a dozen in the Argus to a committee of seven in the dispatch.

reader.title: Threats against Henry Johnson in St. Louis
bases: A group of Marines threatened Johnson at his hotel over his speech and threats by telephone drove him to leave the city in disguise; no injury is reported and he was a visiting speaker, not a resident (A2, A3, A8).

The local Argus (A3) and a separate St. Louis dispatch (A8) both report Marines confronting Johnson to demand he withdraw his remarks, though only the Argus reports the threats and his departure in disguise.

accounts.label: Black local paper (St. Louis Argus)
accounts.gist: About a dozen Marines threatened Johnson at the New Grand Hotel unless he took back what he said about Marine cowardice; he refused, and telephone threats drove him out of the city in disguise that night.

accounts.label: St. Louis dispatch reprinted in the Black press
accounts.gist: Returned white soldiers obtained a federal warrant; deputy marshals deferred arrest when Johnson promised a formal retraction, and more than 100 marines sent a committee of seven to demand he withdraw his charges.

framing.detail: The Argus reported the threats and forced departure in its headline but called Johnson 'Unmanageable in Harangue' and quoted Black leaders disowning him; its editorial said he lacked the sense to appreciate the honor offered.
The Defender ('White Soldiers Accuse Sergt. Johnson of Slander'), Plaindealer ('Called White Yanks Cowards') and Colorado Statesman ran the warrant story without comment.
The Cleveland Advocate reported the speech as a 'fiery account' that 'denounced the white soldiers' and did not mention the aftermath.

versions.value: Johnson refused to take back his remarks, denying he charged the Marines with cowardice
Johnson promised to retract in a formal statement, and arrest was deferred

conflicts.note: The Argus is local and describes the hotel visit; the dispatch describes the marshals' visit. The two may refer to different demands; neither reports what followed.

versions.value: A committee of seven sent by more than 100 marines

conflicts.note: Both describe a delegation of Marines; the numbers differ.

versions.value: He said he threatened to kill a white lieutenant who ran under fire, and denied charging the Marines with cowardice
He was said to have called whites cowards and said the marines refused to fight in the same trenches with Black soldiers

conflicts.note: The dispatch version is attributed ('is said to have said') and comes from the complainants' side.

One person, Sergt. Henry Johnson of Albany, N.Y.
Marines (about a dozen, or a committee of seven for more than 100); returned white soldiers sought a federal warrant
An organized delegation of Marines rather than a mob
Threats and departure in disguise, plus a federal warrant sought on the complaint of white soldiers and deferred arrest
